Broadridge to Bring OnChain Governance and Digital Transfer Agency to New York Stock Exchange Tokenized Securities Platform
summary:
Broadridge  today announced plans to bring on-chain shareholder governance and digital transfer agency services to New York Stock Exchange’s (NYSE) tokenized securities platform, scheduled to launch following regulatory approval. These steps demonstrate the NYSE platform’s interoperability and marks the next phase of its development and Broadridge’s commitment to bringing world class governance and transfer agency services to token investors and public companies.
“Broadridge is building the governance layer for tokenized equities, ensuring investors have access to trusted, institutional-grade governance. We’re pleased to bring these capabilities to the NYSE’s tokenized securities platform. We’re also making it easier for issuers to participate by bringing our digital and traditional transfer agency services and proxy voting capabilities together in one solution—regardless of how shares are traded or where they are held,” said Tim Gokey, CEO of Broadridge.
NYSE will leverage Broadridge’s governance smart contracts, connecting tokenized securities to meeting agendas, voting rules, and verifiable results. The framework supports proxy material distribution and digital wallet authentication linked to verified voting entitlements, helping investors exercise their shareholder rights as ownership moves on-chain. Investors can participate in Broadridge’s on-chain governance services through supported wallets, broker interfaces or ProxyVote, based on their preferences.
“Tokenization has the potential to transform the manner in which issuers interact with their shareholders,” said Lynn Martin, President, NYSE Group. “Onboarding Broadridge’s digital transfer agency service marries trust and innovation, and partnering with NYSE advances our goal of connecting tokenized trading, clearing, and shareholder governance across a more unified ecosystem.”
The integration of Broadridge’s digital transfer agency service expands the NYSE platform’s connectivity with digital transfer agency services, giving issuers greater choice in how they bring their equities on-chain. Broadridge’s services will enable NYSE-listed issuers to tokenize their stock for trading on NYSE’s tokenized securities platform—connecting issuer services with digital trading infrastructure.
The partnership between Broadridge and NYSE brings together stock tokenization, transfer agency services, shareholder communications, proxy voting, and digital identity capabilities to connect tokenized stock ownership with the infrastructure that supports public company governance.

content: Broadridge Financial Solutions announced plans to bring on-chain shareholder governance and digital transfer agency services to the New York Stock Exchange's upcoming tokenized securities platform. The integration will support proxy voting, digital wallet authentication, and issuer services, connecting tokenized stock ownership with traditional public company governance infrastructure following regulatory approval.

24/7 Markets: Are Brokers Ready?
summary:
As trading access extends beyond standard sessions, the operative question for brokers is shifting from what clients can trade to whether the liquidity and execution behind that access can keep up.
Financial markets have long run on fixed trading sessions. Those hours have shaped how brokers manage instrument availability, client support, liquidity, and risk. That pattern is loosening. More products can now be traded outside standard sessions, while selected instruments offer 24/7 market access.
For brokers, the change opens room to widen what they offer and meet shifting client demand. It also raises a practical question: what happens when trading continues past the hours the underlying market normally keeps?
Offering an instrument is the straightforward part. The harder part is everything behind it: pricing, institutional liquidity, how orders are filled and the operations that support them. The question is no longer only what clients can trade, but whether a broker’s own setup is ready for a market that no longer follows the old timetable.
Availability is becoming part of the proposition
Client expectations move with access. Once an instrument can be traded outside standard sessions, clients begin to treat that flexibility as normal, and availability becomes part of what a broker is judged on.
That turns a product decision into an operational one. Extending access can answer real demand, but every instrument has its own characteristics and trading terms. A round-the-clock offering in one product category says nothing about whether another market can, or should, work the same way.
The point matters most where a product gives exposure to an asset whose own market keeps established hours. Extended access to that product may rest on pricing and liquidity arrangements of its own, which belong to that product and should not be read across to other instruments linked to the same asset.
Brokers therefore need to be clear about what is available, when it trades and which terms apply to each 24/7 instrument, and to describe each product for what it is rather than implying blanket access across an asset class. That clarity also helps match a wider range to different client groups: some value flexibility around work hours or time zones, others the ability to react to news that breaks after the close. Either way, the operational demands behind those expectations sit with the broker.
The operational questions behind 24/7 market access
Longer hours change the environment orders are handled in. Liquidity conditions shift across the day, and the depth available in peak sessions may thin out at other times. Those gaps shape how a broker weighs the instruments it lists and the providers standing behind them.
Pricing deserves particular care, because the terms attached to a product depend on its structure and its trading schedule. The characteristics of one product should not be assumed to carry over to another, even when both track a similar underlying asset. Execution calls for the same scrutiny: accepting an order says little about what filling it will look like once participation drops away from peak-session levels. What matters is how orders are handled under the conditions specific to each product and whether those fit the broker’s own requirements.
This becomes most pressing when clients expect access during the quieter stretches outside normal session activity. The assessment has to rest on the specific instrument and how it trades, not on the broad promise of round-the-clock availability.
Liquidity providers adapt alongside brokers
A broker cannot weigh extended access on its own. The institutional partners behind an offering help determine which instruments can be made available and on what terms.
For banks and brokers, access to broad multi-asset liquidity, workable liquidity arrangements and dependable execution feeds directly into decisions about which products to build and how to run them. The needs differ by instrument, by client base and by the institution’s operating model, which makes the choice of partner a question that reaches well past initial market coverage. What counts is understanding the liquidity and execution behind an offering and how a provider supports different products and trading environments.
XTB Institutional provides institutional liquidity and execution access for brokers and banks, backed by the infrastructure and experience of XTB Group. Its offering spans multi-asset market access, reliable execution and relationship-led support for professional market participants. For an institution weighing broader availability, those are among the capabilities that determine how well an expanded offering can be supported.
Inside XTB Institutional’s 24/7 offering
XTB Institutional is extending its round-the-clock range, and the clearest way to read it is product by product, since each has its own structure and trading terms.
The range includes 24/7 CFDs based on tokenised shares such as Google, Tesla, NVIDIA and SpaceX. Separately, it includes a 24/7 GOLD CFD based on tokenised PAX Gold. These are distinct examples rather than a single set of conditions applied across everything, and each should be considered on the terms of the specific product.
For a broker looking at new instruments, that distinction is the practical one. A wider product range can open more ways to serve clients, but each product stands on its own: availability, pricing, liquidity and execution are connected considerations, not interchangeable ones.
Beyond these examples, the wider institutional proposition covers liquidity and execution access, deep order books and multi-asset coverage for brokers and banks. Together they point to the real question, which is how an institution can support changing patterns of access rather than simply list more products.
Readiness requires more than longer hours
Extended and round-the-clock access leaves the industry with a broader question. If clients can trade more instruments outside standard sessions, brokers have to work out how those products sit within their operations and the expectations they set.
That means reading the specific terms of each instrument, understanding the liquidity and execution behind it, and describing the access on offer accurately. It also means judging institutional partners on the instruments and services they can genuinely support. No single model fits every market or product: what a round-the-clock instrument needs depends on how it is built and the terms under which it trades, and treating availability as the whole story risks missing what actually makes an offering work.
For brokers and banks, then, the next phase of market access is as much an operational question as a product one. The institutions best placed for it will be those that understand what each offering demands and can weigh liquidity, pricing and execution next to availability. Markets may be moving towards trading around the clock, but readiness, on the broker’s side, is what will decide who can meet it.

While offering round-the-clock products like tokenized assets meets growing client demand, each instrument requires careful assessment of its specific terms and institutional support to ensure reliable performance beyond standard sessions.
